title: Gwerfyl's Bird Feeder Fix
markdown:
Gwerfyl Button was an otter who loved gears and springs more than most otters loved fish. His workshop sat beside a babbling brook at Meadowbrook Park. Sunlight made dust motes dance. The air smelled of clean oil and old wood. Clocks ticked a soft symphony he trusted more than crowds.

Today a nervous flutter lived under his fur. The Meadowbrook Festival was days away, and with it the Golden Cog, the prize every craftsman in the park dreamed of being seen beside.

For months he had built a self-winding bird feeder clock: tick the hour, then release seeds on time, a clever self-powered thought. He imagined it shining at the festival, quiet skill made visible.

The hitch was small and stubborn. The feeder jammed. Or it spilled a messy waste of seed. Or it held everything back, leaving birds to chirp at an empty tray. Gwerfyl’s whiskers twitched as he flipped his worn notebook. Between clock plans sat other questions: Why do ladybugs always land on the left leaf? Where do shadows go at night? He noticed quiet wonders most people walked past. This jam felt like his largest mystery. The Cog was not only a prize. It was a way not to fade like a forgotten gear, a passing shadow.

Outside, festival preparations buzzed. Banners went up between oaks. Stalls clattered into being. A distant drum set a rhythm that did not match his ticking. He set the clock in a velvet-lined box. Nell the alpaca waited by the door, soft fleece, keen eyes, the right companion for a world that was louder than a workshop.

The grounds were a swirling sea of unfamiliar faces, loud voices, and a hundred smells that were not oil. Gwerfyl set up his display with Nell close enough to lean on. The clock gleamed in dappled light. Competition arrived smelling of gingerbread: a baker’s clock puffed cinnamon with every chime, and children followed their noses. A gardener’s sundial unfurled tiny paper flowers as hours passed, which the crowd understood at once. Gwerfyl’s machine was the most complicated, the most technically impressive, and the hardest to love in a single glance. He explained counterweights and winding paths in a voice a little too soft and a little too full of levers. People nodded kindly and moved toward cinnamon.

Every so often a faint thump ran through the dispenser and sent a jolt through his paws. He adjusted a spring, then a tiny lever. The problem stayed. A gust rattled the case and he flinched. The workshop, for a moment, looked like a better country. He almost packed the velvet box and went home to ticking he could trust.

Then, in a scrap of desperation, he found a counterweight he had not noticed, hidden under a decorative swirl. He held his breath. The clock chimed a clear sweet note. Sunflower seeds streamed into the tray. A small cheer went up. His tail flicked, a rare flag. He had fixed it.

Afternoon, however, is a critic. He watched. A hesitation. A single seed stuck on the dispenser’s edge. The perfect run had been a glimpse. The victory already had a hairline crack.

The awards were grand. Gwerfyl stood by Nell, heart drumming. Gingerbread took third. The sundial took second — no. The announcer boomed a special commendation, then: second-place ribbon to Gwerfyl Button’s Bird Feeder Clock. He blinked. Not the Golden Cog. Something real. He walked forward for a bright blue ribbon. Applause faded. A quiet dust of disappointment settled. He had wanted true perfection and received a near-win that still jammed if you looked long enough.

They packed as the sun went down. The ribbon felt heavier than cloth. He fiddled with the mechanism on the walk home. The unfinished feeling came with him, a guest that did not wipe its feet.

The workshop welcomed them with oil and brass. He set the clock on the bench, ribbon beside it, and cleaned his tools. A rustle. A field mouse crept onto the wood and, with a nudge almost too small to see, touched a lever on the clock’s side — a rice-grain of metal, the very part that had been sticking. The mouse vanished into shadow.

Gwerfyl stared. He had been living in the big gears, the complex story he had designed, and had missed the quietest interaction on the bench. He did not make a speech about it. He touched the little lever himself, gently, the way the mouse had, and the next seed fell clean. Nell’s ears tipped forward. Outside, the brook kept its own time.

He left the blue ribbon on the bench where the mouse had stood. In the morning the birds would find the tray honest. The Cog still belonged to someone else. The left-leaf ladybugs, he suspected, had known the trick all along.
characters: Gwerfyl Button (a patient otter clock repairer), Nell (an alpaca friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
